questions.question: Which key event in the life cycle of Plasmodium causes rupture of red blood cells?

options.text: Sexual reproduction inside mosquitoes in the erythrocytes
Maturation and multiplication of merozoites inside the RBCs

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Maturation and multiplication of merozoites inside the RBCs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Plasmodium merozoites invade red blood cells (RBCs), where they undergo maturation and multiplication.
 
• During the erythrocytic phase, merozoites transform into trophozoites and then schizonts, which contain multiple daughter merozoites.
 
• As schizonts mature, the infected RBCs rupture, releasing numerous merozoites into the bloodstream.
 
• The rupture of RBCs is responsible for the cyclical fever and chills characteristic of malaria.
 
• This process also contributes to anemia due to the destruction of red blood cells.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Plasmodium Life Cycle:**

 
 
• Plasmodium has a complex life cycle involving two hosts: mosquitoes and humans.
 
• The stages include the sporozoite stage in mosquito saliva, liver stage in humans, and erythrocytic stage in human blood.
 
• The erythrocytic stage is responsible for the clinical symptoms of malaria.
 
 
 
• **Role of Merozoites:**
 
 
• Merozoites are the invasive form of Plasmodium that infect RBCs.
 
• They are formed during the liver stage and released into the bloodstream.
 
 
 
• **Malaria Symptoms:**
 
 
• Symptoms include cyclical fever, chills, sweating, headache, and muscle pain.
 
• These symptoms correlate with the rupture of RBCs during the erythrocytic stage.
 
 
 
• **Preventive Measures:**
 
 
• Use of insecticide-treated mosquito nets and indoor residual spraying.
 
• Antimalarial drugs and vaccines are under development for malaria prevention.

questions.question: If HF is a weak acid, what can be inferred about the strength of its conjugate base F⁻?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It is a weak base**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• HF (hydrofluoric acid) is classified as a weak acid because it does not completely dissociate into its ions in an aqueous solution.
 
• According to the Bronsted-Lowry theory, the strength of a conjugate base is inversely related to the strength of its parent acid.
 
• Since HF is a weak acid, its conjugate base (F⁻) has a relatively low tendency to accept protons, making it a **weak base**.
 
• Weak acids like HF have conjugate bases that are stronger than the conjugate bases of strong acids but are still not strong enough to be classified as strong bases.
 
• F⁻ has a modest ability to accept protons due to its high electronegativity, which contributes to its weak basic nature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Acid and Base Strength:**

 
 
• A strong acid dissociates completely in water, producing a negligible conjugate base (e.g., HCl and Cl⁻).
 
• A weak acid only partially dissociates, resulting in a conjugate base with measurable basicity (e.g., HF and F⁻).
 
 
 
• **Conjugate Acid-Base Pairs:**
 
 
• These are pairs of molecules or ions that differ by a single proton (H⁺).
 
• For example, HF (acid) and F⁻ (base) form a conjugate acid-base pair.
 
 
 
• **Role of Electronegativity:**
 
 
• Fluoride ion (F⁻) is highly electronegative, which limits its ability to accept protons, contributing to its weak basicity.
 
 
 
• **pKa and pKb Relationship:**
 
 
• The strength of an acid (pKa) and its conjugate base (pKb) are related: pKa + pKb = 14 (at 25°C).
 
• A weak acid like HF has a higher pKa, so its conjugate base (F⁻) has a lower pKb, indicating weak basicity.
 
 
 
• **Applications of HF and F⁻:**
 
 
• HF is widely used in industrial processes such as glass etching and metal cleaning.
 
• F⁻ is used in fluoride treatments for dental health and in water fluoridation.

questions.question: Deficiency of which nutrient is most directly linked to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Iron**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Iron is an essential nutrient required for the synthesis of hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells responsible for oxygen transport in the body.
 
• Iron deficiency leads to a condition called **iron-deficiency anemia**, which directly reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.
 
• The primary symptoms of iron-deficiency anemia include fatigue, weakness, pale skin, and shortness of breath due to insufficient oxygen supply to tissues.
 
• Dietary sources of iron include red meat, poultry, fish, legumes, leafy green vegetables, and iron-fortified cereals.
 
• Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, whereas substances like calcium and phytates can inhibit its absorption.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hemoglobin:**

 
 
• Hemoglobin is a protein in red blood cells that binds to oxygen in the lungs and transports it to tissues throughout the body.
 
• Each hemoglobin molecule contains iron, which is critical for its oxygen-binding capacity.
 
 
 
• **Iron-Deficiency Anemia:**
 
 
• A condition where the body lacks sufficient iron to produce adequate amounts of hemoglobin.
 
• It is the most common type of anemia globally and can affect people of all ages.
 
 
 
• **Types of Iron:**
 
 
• Heme iron: Found in animal-based foods like meat and is more easily absorbed by the body.
 
• Non-heme iron: Found in plant-based foods and has lower bioavailability compared to heme iron.
 
 
 
• **Iron Absorption:**
 
 
• Vitamin C-rich foods like oranges and tomatoes enhance iron absorption.
 
• Calcium, tea, coffee, and whole grains may inhibit iron absorption when consumed together with iron-rich foods.
 
 
 
• **Prevention and Treatment:**
 
 
• Preventing iron deficiency involves consuming a balanced diet rich in iron and vitamin C.
 
• Iron supplements may be prescribed in cases of severe deficiency, under medical supervision.

questions.question: A sound wave with a period of 0.01 seconds has a frequency of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**100 Hz**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The relationship between frequency and period is defined as **Frequency = 1 / Period**.
 
• A sound wave with a period of 0.01 seconds has a frequency calculated as **1 / 0.01 = 100 Hz**.
 
• Frequency is measured in **Hertz (Hz)**, which represents the number of cycles per second.
 
• Sound waves with a frequency of 100 Hz fall within the range of **human hearing, typically between 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.**
 
• The period and frequency are inversely related—if the period is short, the frequency is high, and vice versa.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Frequency:**

 
 
• Frequency refers to the number of oscillations or cycles a wave completes in one second.
 
• It is measured in Hertz (Hz), where 1 Hz equals one cycle per second.
 
 
 
• **Period:**
 
 
• The period is the time taken for one complete cycle of a wave.
 
• It is expressed in seconds and is the reciprocal of frequency.
 
 
 
• **Sound Waves:**
 
 
• Sound waves are longitudinal waves that travel through a medium (air, water, solids).
 
• They consist of compressions and rarefactions caused by vibrating objects.
 
 
 
• **Human Hearing Range:**
 
 
• Humans can typically hear frequencies ranging from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
 
• Frequencies below 20 Hz are called infrasonic, and frequencies above 20,000 Hz are ultrasonic.

questions.question: In lipid biochemistry, why do unsaturated fatty acids tend to be liquid at room temperature?

options.text: They form ionic bonds that prevent solidification.
The cis-double bonds introduce kinks, reducing van der Waals interactions.
Their double bonds increase molecular symmetry leading to less crystal packing.
They have lower molecular weights than saturated fatty acids.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The cis-double bonds introduce kinks, reducing van der Waals interactions.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Unsaturated fatty acids have **cis-double bonds** that introduce kinks in their hydrocarbon chains.
 
• These kinks prevent tight packing of the fatty acid molecules, thereby **reducing van der Waals interactions**.
 
• As a result, unsaturated fatty acids have **lower melting points** compared to saturated fatty acids, making them liquid at room temperature.
 
• The inability to tightly pack molecules leads to a more **fluid structure**, which is characteristic of oils derived from unsaturated fatty acids.
 
• The degree of unsaturation (number of double bonds) further influences the extent of fluidity in these molecules.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Van der Waals interactions:**

 
 
• These are weak forces of attraction between molecules due to temporary dipoles.
 
• In saturated fatty acids, tight packing results in stronger van der Waals forces, contributing to solid state at room temperature.
 
 
 
• **Cis and trans configurations:**
 
 
• Cis-double bonds introduce bends or kinks in the fatty acid chains, while trans-double bonds allow linear structures.
 
• Trans fats behave more like saturated fats and are often solid at room temperature.
 
 
 
• **Saturated vs Unsaturated Fatty Acids:**
 
 
• Saturated fatty acids lack double bonds, allowing tighter molecular packing.
 
• Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more double bonds, which disrupt packing and increase fluidity.
 
 
 
• **Role in cell membranes:**
 
 
• Unsaturated fatty acids contribute to membrane fluidity, essential for cellular functions.
 
• Phospholipids with unsaturated fatty acid tails are a key component of biological membranes.
 
 
 
• **Melting points of fatty acids:**
 
 
• Saturated fatty acids like stearic acid have higher melting points.
 
• Unsaturated fatty acids like oleic acid are liquid at room temperature due to disrupted packing.

questions.question: At STP, the number of molecules present in 5.6 L of O2 gas is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1.5055 x 10²³**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• At standard temperature and pressure (STP), 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies a volume of **22.4 L**.
 
• The number of molecules in 1 mole of a substance is given by **Avogadro's number = 6.022 x 10²³**.
 
• Given volume = 5.6 L, which corresponds to **5.6 ÷ 22.4 = 0.25 moles**.
 
• The number of molecules in 0.25 moles can be calculated as **0.25 x 6.022 x 10²³ = 1.5055 x 10²³**.
 
• Thus, the correct answer is **1.05055 x 10²³**, i.e., Option 4.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Standard Temperature and Pressure (STP):**

 
 
• STP refers to conditions where the temperature is 0°C (273.15 K) and the pressure is 1 atmosphere (101.325 kPa).
 
• Under these conditions, 1 mole of an ideal gas occupies a volume of 22.4 L.
 
 
 
• **Avogadro's Number:**
 
 
• It is the number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions) in 1 mole of a substance.
 
• The value of Avogadro's number is approximately **6.022 x 10²³**.
 
 
 
• **Mole Concept:**
 
 
• A mole is a fundamental unit in chemistry representing the quantity of substance.
 
• It is used to relate the mass of a substance to the number of particles it contains.
 
 
 
• **Ideal Gas Law:**
 
 
• The ideal gas law is expressed as PV = nRT, where P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = gas constant, and T = temperature.
 
• Under STP conditions, the molar volume of an ideal gas is fixed at 22.4 L.

questions.question: Chemical fertilisers were used intensively during the Green Revolution. What was the result of their overuse?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Soil salinity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Intensive use of chemical fertilizers** during the Green Revolution led to an increase in soil salinity, negatively impacting agricultural productivity.
 
• High levels of fertilizers, especially nitrogen-based ones, can disrupt soil chemistry, reducing its ability to retain water and nutrients.
 
• **Soil salinity affects crop growth** by restricting the plants' ability to absorb water and essential nutrients due to osmotic stress.
 
• Regions practicing intensive farming with chemical inputs, such as Punjab and Haryana, reported significant degradation of soil health due to salinity.
 
• Efforts to mitigate soil salinity include techniques like organic farming, crop rotation, and the use of bio-fertilizers to restore soil health.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Soil Salinity:**

 
 
• It refers to the accumulation of soluble salts in the soil, which can harm plant growth and soil health.
 
• Saline soils are often characterized by white crusts and reduced agricultural yield.
 
 
 
• **Green Revolution:**
 
 
• A period during the 1960s-70s marked by increased agricultural production due to modern techniques, including high-yield crop varieties and chemical fertilizers.
 
• While it solved food shortages, it had environmental consequences such as soil degradation and water table depletion.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Chemical Fertilizers:**
 
 
• Excessive use can lead to nutrient imbalance and pollution in nearby water bodies due to runoff.
 
• Prolonged use may reduce microbial diversity in soil, further degrading its quality.
 
 
 
• **Sustainable Farming Practices:**
 
 
• Techniques such as organic farming, agroforestry, and precision agriculture promote soil health.
 
• Bio-fertilizers and natural compost are alternatives to chemical fertilizers for sustainable agriculture.

questions.question: What does PCB stand for in electronics?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Printed Circuit Board**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A **Printed Circuit Board (PCB)** is a non-conductive board that holds and connects electronic components using conductive pathways, pads, and tracks etched from copper sheets.
 
• PCBs are used in almost all electronic devices, including mobile phones, computers, televisions, and industrial equipment.
 
• They are essential for simplifying and streamlining the manufacturing and assembly process of electronic circuits.
 
• PCBs can be single-layered, double-layered, or multi-layered, depending on the complexity of the circuit and application.
 
• PCBs replaced traditional wire-based circuits, making devices more compact, efficient, and reliable.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Components of a PCB:**

 
 
• **Substrate:** The base material, usually fiberglass, providing the board's rigidity.
 
• **Copper Layer:** Conductive layer used for electrical connections.
 
• **Solder Mask:** Protective layer applied over the copper to prevent short circuits.
 
• **Silkscreen:** Layer for labeling components and providing assembly guidance.
 
 
 
• **Types of PCBs:**
 
 
• **Single-Sided PCBs:** Copper traces are present only on one side of the board.
 
• **Double-Sided PCBs:** Copper traces exist on both sides, interconnected by vias.
 
• **Multi-Layered PCBs:** Composed of multiple layers of copper and insulating material.
 
 
 
• **Advantages of PCBs:**
 
 
• Compact and lightweight design, leading to smaller electronic devices.
 
• Increased reliability due to reduced wiring complexity and consistent manufacturing.
 
• Cost-effective in mass production.
 
 
 
• **Applications of PCBs:**
 
 
• Consumer electronics like smartphones, laptops, and televisions.
 
• Automotive systems, including sensors and control modules.
 
• Medical devices such as pacemakers and imaging systems.
 
• Industrial equipment used in manufacturing and robotics.

questions.question: Which of the following is a unit of the dimension 'length'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Metre**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Metre** is the fundamental unit of length in the International System of Units (SI).
 
• It is defined as the distance traveled by light in a vacuum in **1/299,792,458 seconds**.
 
• The metre is widely used for measuring distance, height, and dimensions in scientific and everyday applications.
 
• Other units of length such as kilometer, centimeter, and millimeter are derived from the metre.
 
• The adoption of the metre as the standard unit of length ensures consistency in measurements globally.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **International System of Units (SI):**

 
 
• SI is the modern form of the metric system and is the most widely used system of measurement worldwide.
 
• It comprises seven base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (electric current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), and candela (luminous intensity).
 
 
 
• **Derived Units:**
 
 
• Units derived from the base units include area (square metre), volume (cubic metre), and velocity (metres per second).
 
• Derived units are used for more complex measurements and calculations in science and engineering.
 
 
 
• **Non-SI Units:**
 
 
• Non-SI units like inch, foot, and mile are still used in certain countries, primarily the United States.
 
• Conversion between SI and non-SI units is necessary for global standardization.
 
 
 
• **Historical Evolution of the Metre:**
 
 
• The metre was originally defined in 1793 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole along a meridian.
 
• Advancements in technology led to its redefinition based on the speed of light in 1983.

questions.question: In a dicot root, which tissue(s) is/are found between the xylem and phloem?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Conjunctive tissue**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In a dicot root, **conjunctive tissue** is a type of parenchymatous tissue that is located between the xylem and phloem.
 
• The conjunctive tissue plays a critical role in providing **mechanical support** to the vascular bundles.
 
• It is composed of living cells, primarily parenchyma, which help in the storage of food substances.
 
• The arrangement of xylem and phloem in dicot roots is **radial**, and the conjunctive tissue fills the space between these vascular tissues.
 
• This tissue also contributes to the formation of **vascular cambium** during secondary growth in dicot roots.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dicot Root Anatomy:**

 
 
• Dicot roots have a distinct arrangement of tissues: epidermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, vascular bundles, and pith.
 
• The vascular bundles are arranged in a radial pattern, with xylem and phloem alternating around the center.
 
 
 
• **Radial Vascular Bundles:**
 
 
• In radial vascular bundles, xylem and phloem are present on different radii, separated by conjunctive tissue.
 
 
 
• **Role of Vascular Cambium:**
 
 
• The vascular cambium originates from the conjunctive tissue during secondary growth, contributing to the formation of secondary xylem and phloem.
 
 
 
• **Parenchyma in Roots:**
 
 
• Parenchyma cells in the conjunctive tissue are living, thin-walled, and capable of storing nutrients.
 
• They also play a role in repair and regeneration of tissues in plants.

questions.question: According to the first law of reflection, all the incident ray, the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence and the reflected ray:

options.text: are mutually perpendicular to each other

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**lie in the same plane**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first law of reflection states that the incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal to the surface of the mirror at the point of incidence **all lie in the same plane**.
 
• This law applies to any reflecting surface, including plane, concave, or convex mirrors.
 
• The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, but this relationship is valid only if the rays and the normal lie in the same plane.
 
• **This fundamental principle ensures predictability in the behavior of light during reflection** and is crucial for understanding optics.
 
• [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reflection of Light:**

 
 
• Reflection is the phenomenon of light bouncing back into the same medium after striking a smooth surface.
 
• It is governed by two laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and all rays and the normal lie in the same plane.
 
 
 
• **Normal:**
 
 
• A normal is a perpendicular line drawn to the surface at the point of incidence.
 
• It serves as the reference line for measuring the angles of incidence and reflection.
 
 
 
• **Angle of Incidence and Reflection:**
 
 
• The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the normal.
 
• The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
 
 
 
• **Types of Reflection:**
 
 
• **Regular Reflection:** Occurs on smooth surfaces, producing clear images.
 
• **Diffuse Reflection:** Occurs on rough surfaces, scattering light in different directions.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Reflection:**
 
 
• Used in mirrors, optical instruments like telescopes, and periscopes.
 
• Fundamental to the working of devices like rearview mirrors and solar reflectors.

questions.question: What makes DNA the most abundant genetic material?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Its stable double-helical structure**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **double-helical structure** of DNA is stabilized by hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous bases and hydrophobic interactions among the base pairs.
 
• This stable structure ensures the **faithful replication** and preservation of genetic information across generations.
 
• The stability of DNA allows it to resist degradation and maintain its integrity, making it the most **abundant genetic material**.
 
• The backbone of DNA is made up of **phosphate and deoxyribose sugar**, which contributes to its chemical resilience.
 
• The structure also facilitates the precise pairing of bases (adenine with thymine, and cytosine with guanine), ensuring **accurate genetic coding**.
 
• The stability of DNA is further enhanced by its ability to interact with **histones and other proteins**, which help compact and protect it within chromosomes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• ** Its high mutation rate**__

 __
 
• A high mutation rate would make DNA unstable and less reliable for preserving genetic information.
 
• While mutations play a role in evolution, excessive mutations can lead to **genetic disorders** and errors in replication.
 
 
 
• **Its interaction with proteins**__
 __
 
• DNA interacts with proteins like histones to form chromatin; however, this feature is not directly responsible for DNA being the most abundant genetic material.
 
• Protein interactions primarily help in **packaging and regulation** of genetic material.
 
 
 
• **Its enzymatic roles**__
 
 
• DNA itself does not perform enzymatic roles; instead, enzymes like DNA polymerase and helicase act on DNA during replication and repair.
 
• Enzymatic roles are more relevant to **RNA**, which can act as a ribozyme (catalytic RNA).

questions.question: Who discovered the antibacterial properties of a Penicillium fungus in 1929?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Alexander Fleming**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Alexander Fleming** discovered the antibacterial properties of a **Penicillium fungus** in **1929**.
 
• He observed that a mold, later identified as **Penicillium notatum**, had killed bacteria surrounding it in a petri dish.
 
• This discovery led to the development of **penicillin**, the world’s first widely effective antibiotic.
 
• **Penicillin** was instrumental in treating bacterial infections during **World War II**, saving countless lives.
 
• Fleming’s work earned him the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine** in **1945**, shared with **Ernst Boris Chain** and **Howard Florey**, who helped mass-produce penicillin.
 
• Penicillin revolutionized medicine and is considered one of the greatest discoveries in the field of **microbiology and pharmacology.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Paul Ehrlich**__

 __
 
• **Paul Ehrlich** was a German scientist known for his work on **immunology** and the development of the first chemotherapy agent.
 
• He discovered the drug **Salvarsan**, which was used to treat **syphilis**.
 
• Ehrlich introduced the concept of a "**magic bullet**"—a drug that could target disease-causing organisms without harming the host.
 
 
 
• **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek**__
 __
 
• **Antonie van Leeuwenhoek** was a Dutch scientist who is known as the "**Father of Microbiology**."
 
• He was the first to observe and describe **microorganisms**, such as bacteria and protozoa, using a microscope.
 
• His discoveries laid the foundation for the field of **microbiology**.
 
 
 
• **Marie Curie**__
 
 
• **Marie Curie** was a Polish-French scientist known for her groundbreaking research on **radioactivity**.
 
• She was the first woman to win a **Nobel Prize** and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics and Chemistry).
 
• Her discoveries of **radium** and **polonium** were instrumental in the development of nuclear science and medicine.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is NOT correct with reference to the modern periodic table?

options.text: ​Lanthanoids and actinoids are placed in separate panels at the bottom.
Groups are the vertical columns, and periods are horizontal rows.
The second and third periods each contain 8 elements.

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**The first period contains 8 elements.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **modern periodic table** arranges elements based on their **atomic numbers** in horizontal rows called **periods** and vertical columns called **groups.**
 
• The **first period** of the modern periodic table contains only **two elements: Hydrogen and Helium.**
 
• This is because the first energy level (shell) can hold a maximum of **two electrons.**
 
• Thus, the statement that the first period contains **8 elements** is incorrect.
 
• Subsequent periods contain more elements due to the increasing capacity of energy levels to hold electrons.
 
• For example, the **second period** contains **8 elements**, corresponding to the filling of the 2s and 2p orbitals.
 
• The periodic table is divided into blocks based on the **sub-shells** being filled (s, p, d, f blocks).
 
• The placement of elements reflects their **properties** and provides a systematic way to study chemical behavior.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lanthanoids and actinoids are placed in separate panels at the bottom**__

 __
 
• **Lanthanoids** and **actinoids** are the f-block elements of the periodic table.
 
• They are placed separately to maintain the **structure and readability** of the table.
 
• **Lanthanoids** are elements with atomic numbers 57 to 71, while **actinoids** are elements with atomic numbers 89 to 103.
 
• These elements exhibit **unique electronic configurations** and properties, such as their use in **magnets, lasers, and nuclear reactors.**
 
 
 
• **Groups are the vertical columns, and periods are horizontal rows**__
 __
 
• The modern periodic table has **18 groups** and **7 periods.**
 
• **Groups** are vertical columns where elements have similar **valence electron configurations** and chemical properties.
 
• **Periods** are horizontal rows representing elements with increasing atomic numbers.
 
• For example, elements in Group 1 are the **alkali metals,** while those in Group 17 are the **halogens.**
 
 
 
• **The second and third periods each contain 8 elements**__
 
 
• The **second period** contains elements from **Lithium to Neon**, corresponding to the filling of 2s and 2p orbitals.
 
• The **third period** contains elements from **Sodium to Argon**, corresponding to the filling of 3s and 3p orbitals.
 
• This pattern reflects the **quantum mechanical arrangement of electrons** in atoms.

questions.question: The complete sequencing of the human genome has marked the beginning of:
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Genomics**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Genomics** is the study of the entire set of genes (genome) of an organism, including their structure, function, and evolution.
 
• The completion of the **Human Genome Project** in 2003 marked the beginning of genomics.
 
• The **Human Genome Project** was a global scientific research initiative aimed at sequencing the entire human genome, consisting of approximately **3 billion DNA base pairs.**
 
• Genomics enables researchers to understand the **role of genes** in various biological processes, diseases, and traits.
 
• Applications of genomics include **personalized medicine, drug discovery, biotechnology, and agricultural improvements.**
 
• In personalized medicine, genomics helps identify **genetic markers** for diseases, enabling targeted treatments and preventive measures.
 
• Genomics also contributes to understanding **evolutionary biology** by comparing genomes across different species.
 
• It has paved the way for advanced technologies such as **CRISPR gene editing, transcriptomics, and proteomics.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Immunology**__

 __
 
• **Immunology** is the branch of biology that studies the immune system, its functions, and disorders.
 
• It focuses on understanding how the body defends itself against **pathogens** such as viruses, bacteria, and parasites.
 
• Applications of immunology include **vaccine development, immunotherapy, and diagnosing autoimmune diseases.**
 
• While immunology is crucial in healthcare, it is not directly related to genome sequencing.
 
 
 
• **Cytogenetics**__
 __
 
• **Cytogenetics** is the study of chromosomes, their structure, and their role in heredity and diseases.
 
• It involves techniques like **karyotyping** to detect chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome and Turner syndrome.
 
• Cytogenetics is more focused on the physical aspects of chromosomes rather than whole-genome sequencing.
 
 
 
• **Structural Biology**__
 
 
• **Structural Biology** is the study of the molecular structure and dynamics of biological macromolecules like proteins and nucleic acids.
 
• It employs techniques such as **X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, and cryo-electron microscopy.**
 
• While structural biology contributes to understanding biological processes, it does not encompass the entire genome.

questions.question: The coordination number of atoms in a body-centered cubic (BCC) lattice is:
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**8**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **coordination number** refers to the number of nearest neighbor atoms surrounding a particular atom in a crystal lattice.
 
• In a **body-centered cubic (BCC)** lattice, each atom is surrounded by **8 nearest neighbors**.
 
• The BCC structure consists of atoms located at the **corners of the cube** and one atom at the **center of the cube**.
 
• Each corner atom is shared among **8 adjacent unit cells**, while the central atom belongs entirely to the unit cell.
 
• The coordination number of 8 arises from the geometry of the lattice, where the central atom is equidistant from the 8 corner atoms.
 
• This arrangement is commonly found in metals like **iron, chromium, and tungsten**, which adopt the BCC structure.
 
• The BCC lattice is less densely packed compared to other structures like **face-centered cubic (FCC)** or **hexagonal close-packed (HCP)**, but it provides good mechanical stability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **6**__

 __
 
• A coordination number of **6** is typically observed in structures like the **simple cubic lattice**.
 
• In the simple cubic lattice, each atom is surrounded by **6 nearest neighbors**, positioned along the faces of the cube.
 
• This structure is relatively rare in nature due to its low packing efficiency.
 
 
 
• **4**__
 __
 
• A coordination number of **4** is common in structures like **diamond cubic lattices**, where atoms form tetrahedral bonds.
 
• It is observed in materials like **silicon** and **diamond**, which exhibit strong covalent bonding.
 
 
 
• **12**__
 
 
• A coordination number of **12** is observed in densely packed structures like **face-centered cubic (FCC)** and **hexagonal close-packed (HCP)** lattices.
 
• These structures are highly efficient in packing and are commonly found in metals like **gold, aluminum, and copper**.
 
• The high coordination number contributes to their exceptional mechanical and thermal properties.

questions.question: What is the unit of measurement for frequenсу?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Hertz (Hz)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Hertz (Hz)** is the **SI unit of frequency**, which measures the number of cycles of a periodic wave per second.
 
• It is named after the German physicist **Heinrich Rudolf Hertz**, who made significant contributions to the understanding of electromagnetic waves.
 
• 1 Hertz represents **one cycle per second**. For example, a frequency of 50 Hz means there are 50 cycles of the wave occurring each second.
 
• The unit is widely used in various fields such as **physics, telecommunications, acoustics, and electronics** to describe the frequency of waves, including sound waves, electromagnetic waves, and alternating current.
 
• Applications of frequency measurement in **Hertz** include **radio broadcasting** (e.g., FM radio operates at 88-108 MHz), **electricity** (standard power supply frequency is 50 Hz or 60 Hz), and **digital systems** (e.g., processor clock speeds in GHz).
 
• The **Hertz** is a derived unit, and its dimensional formula is **T⁻¹**, where T represents time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Millisecond**__

 __
 
• A **millisecond** (ms) is a unit of time and is equal to **one-thousandth of a second** (1 ms = 0.001 seconds).
 
• It is commonly used in fields like **computer science** and **electronics** to measure short time intervals, such as **response times**.
 
 
 
• **Pascal**__
 __
 
• The **Pascal (Pa)** is the SI unit of **pressure**, not frequency.
 
• It is defined as **one newton per square meter** (1 Pa = 1 N/m²).
 
• This unit is used to measure pressure in various fields such as **fluid dynamics, meteorology, and material science**.
 
 
 
• **Joule**__
 
 
• The **Joule (J)** is the SI unit of **energy**, not frequency.
 
• It is defined as the **work done** when a force of one newton moves an object one meter (1 J = 1 N·m).
 
• It is used in fields like **physics, engineering, and thermodynamics** to measure energy, work, or heat.

questions.question: Which type of muscle fibres are primarily found in the gastrointestinal tract, and what is a key characteristic of their contraction?

options.text: Skeletal muscle fibres, rapid and voluntary contraction
Cardiac muscle fibres, rhythmic and involuntary contraction
Striated muscle fibres, intermittent and forceful contraction
Smooth muscle fibres, slow and sustained involuntary contraction

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 4,Key Points

 
• Muscle fibres in the gastrointestinal tract are primarily **smooth muscle fibres**, which are essential for its function.
 
• **Smooth muscle fibres** are responsible for slow, sustained, and involuntary contractions that facilitate processes like peristalsis.
 
• These fibres are **non-striated**, meaning they lack the organized sarcomere structure seen in skeletal and cardiac muscles.
 
• Smooth muscle contractions are regulated by the **autonomic nervous system**, making them involuntary.
 
• They play a crucial role in the movement of food, absorption, and digestion within the gastrointestinal tract.

Additional Information

 
• **Skeletal Muscle Fibres**

 
 
• Skeletal muscles are striated and under voluntary control.
 
• They are responsible for movement and posture through rapid and forceful contractions.
 
• They are attached to bones via tendons.
 
 
 
• **Cardiac Muscle Fibres**
 
 
• Cardiac muscles are striated and involuntary.
 
• They are exclusively found in the heart and are responsible for rhythmic contractions.
 
• Contractions are regulated by pacemaker cells and the autonomic nervous system.
 
 
 
• **Peristalsis**
 
 
• A wave-like motion produced by smooth muscle contractions in the gastrointestinal tract.
 
• It helps in propelling food and digestive contents forward.
 
 
 
• **Autonomic Nervous System (ANS)**
 
 
• ANS controls involuntary functions in the body, including smooth muscle activity.
 
• The ANS consists of the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

questions.concept: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct with reference to the representative elements?

options.text: They consist of both s- and p-block elements
They are also called Transuranium elements.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2,

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Representative elements include elements from both the **s-block** (Groups 1 and 2) and the **p-block** (Groups 13 to 18) of the periodic table.
 
• These elements are characterized by having their outermost electrons in s- or p-orbitals, which define their chemical properties.
 
• Representative elements encompass a wide range of elements, including **metals, nonmetals, and metalloids**.
 
• Examples of representative elements include **hydrogen, sodium (s-block), and chlorine (p-block)**.
 
• They are distinct from **transition elements**, which have partially filled d-orbitals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__

 
• **s-block elements:** These include alkali metals (Group 1) and alkaline earth metals (Group 2). They are characterized by their high reactivity, low ionization energy, and the presence of electrons in the s-orbital.
 
• **p-block elements:** Found in Groups 13 to 18, p-block elements include metals, nonmetals, and metalloids, and exhibit diverse properties such as variable oxidation states and covalent bonding.
 
• **Transition elements:** These are found in the d-block (Groups 3 to 12) and are distinguished by their partially filled d-orbitals, leading to properties like variable oxidation states and the formation of colored compounds.
 
• **Periodic table structure:** The periodic table is divided into blocks based on the type of orbital being filled (s-block, p-block, d-block, and f-block). Representative elements are part of the s- and p-blocks.
 
• **Metalloids:** Some representative elements, such as silicon and boron, are classified as metalloids and exhibit properties intermediate between metals and nonmetals.
tags: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

questions.concept: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question: What does the horizontal row in the periodic table represent?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2,

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A horizontal row in the periodic table is known as a **period.**
 
• Periods indicate the **principal energy level** or shell that the electrons occupy for a given element.
 
• There are **7 periods** in the modern periodic table, ranging from Period 1 to Period 7.
 
• As we move from left to right across a period, the **atomic number increases sequentially**, meaning the number of protons in the nucleus increases.
 
• Elements in the same period exhibit a gradual variation in properties such as **atomic radius, ionization energy, and electronegativity.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Groups vs. Periods:**

 
 
• **Groups:** Vertical columns in the periodic table, categorized into 18 groups, represent elements with similar chemical properties.
 
• **Periods:** Horizontal rows where properties change progressively across the row due to increasing atomic number.
 
 
 
• **Periodic Trends:** Trends such as atomic size, ionization energy, and electronegativity change across a period due to increasing nuclear charge.
 
• **Electron Configuration:** Elements in a period have electrons filling the same principal energy level (shell).
 
• **Periodic Table Organization:** The periodic table is based on the periodic law, which states that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
 
• **Lanthanides and Actinides:** These form part of Periods 6 and 7, placed separately at the bottom of the table for better visualization.
tags: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the functional diversity of RNA molecules in cells?

options.text: Their capability to act as adapter, structural and catalytic molecules
Their permanent role as genetic material
Their ability to form double-stranded helical structures

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Their capability to act as adapter, structural and catalytic molecules**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• RNA molecules exhibit functional diversity by acting as **adapter molecules** in translation, such as transfer RNA (tRNA), which brings amino acids to the ribosome.
 
• They serve as **structural components** in cellular machinery, such as ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which forms the core of ribosomes.
 
• RNA molecules can act as **catalysts**, such as ribozymes, which facilitate biochemical reactions without being proteins.
 
• RNA plays regulatory roles, such as microRNAs (miRNAs) and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), which modulate gene expression post-transcriptionally.
 
• The versatility of RNA is due to its ability to adopt complex secondary and tertiary structures, enabling diverse functional roles in cellular processes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Messenger RNA (mRNA):**

 
 
• Acts as a template for protein synthesis during translation.
 
• mRNA carries genetic information from DNA to ribosomes.
 
• Each mRNA sequence specifies the amino acid sequence of a protein.
 
 
 
• **Transfer RNA (tRNA):**
 
 
• tRNA functions as an adapter molecule in translation.
 
• It has anticodons that pair with mRNA codons and carries specific amino acids to the ribosome.
 
• tRNA’s cloverleaf structure is critical for its role in protein synthesis.
 
 
 
• **Ribosomal RNA (rRNA):**
 
 
• Forms the structural and functional core of ribosomes.
 
• rRNA helps in aligning mRNA and tRNA during translation.
 
• Some rRNA molecules exhibit catalytic activity, facilitating peptide bond formation.
 
 
 
• **Ribozymes:**
 
 
• RNA molecules with enzymatic properties.
 
• Examples include self-splicing introns and the RNA component of RNase P.
 
• Ribozymes demonstrate that RNA can act as both genetic material and a catalyst.

questions.question: Let’s denote Z as the number of atoms per unit cell, M as the molar mass of the substance, and NA as Avogadro’s number. Which formula is used to calculate the density (d) of a unit cell?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**d = (Z × M) / (a³ × NA)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The formula **d = (Z × M) / (a³ × NA)** is used to calculate the density of a unit cell in crystallography.
 
• In this formula, **Z** represents the number of atoms per unit cell, **M** is the molar mass of the substance, **a³** is the volume of the unit cell (edge length cubed), and **NA** is Avogadro’s number.
 
• The density (d) is expressed in grams per cubic centimeter (g/cm³) when the molar mass is in grams per mole and the unit cell volume is in cubic centimeters.
 
• This formula is derived from the relationship between mass, volume, and density, considering the number of atoms within the unit cell and their molar mass.
 
• It is widely used to predict the crystal structure and verify experimental density measurements in solid-state chemistry and materials science.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Unit Cell:**

 
 
• The unit cell is the smallest repeating structure in a crystal lattice that represents the entire crystal.
 
• Its dimensions are defined by the lengths of edges (a, b, c) and angles between them (α, β, γ).
 
 
 
• **Avogadro’s Number (NA):**
 
 
• Avogadro’s number is approximately **6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹**, representing the number of entities in one mole of a substance.
 
• It is crucial for converting between macroscopic and molecular scales in chemistry.
 
 
 
• **Molar Mass (M):**
 
 
• The molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole (g/mol).
 
• It is calculated as the sum of the atomic masses of all the elements in a compound.
 
 
 
• **Crystal Lattice:**
 
 
• A crystal lattice is a three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, ions, or molecules in a structured and repeating pattern.
 
• Common types of unit cells include cubic, tetragonal, hexagonal, and orthorhombic systems.
 
 
 
• **Density in Crystals:**
 
 
• Density is a physical property that correlates the mass of a substance to its volume.
 
• In crystallography, density helps determine the packing efficiency and arrangement of atoms within a unit cell.

questions.question: Which industries commonly used Tetrachloromethane as a degreasing agent?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Manufacturing and mechanical industries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tetrachloromethane (carbon tetrachloride)** is commonly utilized in manufacturing and mechanical industries due to its excellent degreasing properties.
 
• This compound is effective in removing grease, oil, and other contaminants from metal surfaces, tools, and machinery.
 
• Mechanical industries employ it for cleaning parts during assembly, maintenance, and repair tasks.
 
• Its non-flammable nature made it a preferred choice in industrial applications before its usage was restricted due to environmental concerns.
 
• Industries like aerospace and automotive heavily relied on Tetrachloromethane for degreasing metal components.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tetrachloromethane (Carbon Tetrachloride):**

 
 
• A chemical compound with the formula CCl₄.
 
• Historically used as a solvent, cleaning agent, and refrigerant.
 
• Its use has significantly declined due to its adverse health effects and contribution to ozone layer depletion.
 
 
 
• **Degreasing Agents:**
 
 
• Chemical substances used to remove grease, oil, or dirt from surfaces.
 
• Examples include organic solvents, alkaline solutions, and detergents.
 
• They are widely applied in industries for cleaning machinery, tools, and metal parts.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Concerns:**
 
 
• Carbon Tetrachloride is classified as a potent ozone-depleting substance under the Montreal Protocol.
 
• Its production and use have been phased out in many countries due to its harmful environmental effects.
 
• It is also considered a hazardous air pollutant with serious health risks to humans.
 
 
 
• **Alternative Degreasing Solutions:**
 
 
• Eco-friendly alternatives include water-based cleaners and biodegradable solvents.
 
• Industries are increasingly adopting non-toxic and sustainable cleaning agents.
 
• These alternatives help reduce health risks and environmental impact.

questions.question: Why is the common cold rarely considered a lower respiratory tract infection?

options.text: The virus is destroyed in the alveoli.
It requires a vector for lower tract transmission.
Rhinoviruses only infect the upper respiratory tract.
Antibodies prevent it from entering the lungs.

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Rhinoviruses only infect the upper respiratory tract**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rhinoviruses** are the primary cause of the common cold and are responsible for more than 50% of cases.
 
• These viruses preferentially infect the **upper respiratory tract**, such as the nasal passages and throat.
 
• The upper respiratory tract provides a more suitable environment for rhinoviruses because of its **lower temperature (about 33°C)**, which is optimal for their replication.
 
• The lower respiratory tract, including the lungs and alveoli, generally has a **higher temperature** (around 37°C), which is less conducive for rhinovirus survival and replication.
 
• Rhinoviruses lack mechanisms to effectively invade deeper tissues like the lungs or lower respiratory tract.
 
• Infections caused by rhinoviruses are typically mild and self-limiting, targeting the **mucosal surfaces of the upper respiratory tract**.
 
• Other viruses, such as influenza or respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), are more likely to cause lower respiratory tract infections.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The virus is destroyed in the alveoli**__

 __
 
• The alveoli are small air sacs in the lungs that are involved in oxygen exchange. While certain viruses may struggle to survive in this environment, this is not the primary reason the common cold is rarely a lower respiratory tract infection.
 
• Rhinoviruses do not typically reach the alveoli due to their preference for the upper respiratory tract.
 
 
 
• **It requires a vector for lower tract transmission**__
 __
 
• Rhinoviruses are transmitted via **direct contact**, airborne droplets, or contaminated surfaces, not through a vector like mosquitoes or ticks.
 
• Vector transmission is more commonly associated with diseases like malaria or dengue.
 
 
 
• **Antibodies prevent it from entering the lungs**__
 
 
• While the immune system, including **antibodies**, plays a role in combating infections, the inability of rhinoviruses to infect the lower respiratory tract is primarily due to environmental and biological factors, not antibody interference.
 
• Antibodies are produced as part of the body's response to infection and do not specifically block rhinoviruses from entering the lungs.

questions.question: Which force acts without physical contact and governs celestial body motion in mechanics?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Gravitational Force**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gravitational Force** is a fundamental force that acts without physical contact.
 
• It governs the motion of **celestial bodies** such as planets, stars, and moons.
 
• This force is responsible for holding objects in their **orbits**, such as the Earth revolving around the Sun or the Moon orbiting the Earth.
 
• The force is described by **Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation**, which states that every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
 
• Gravitational force is always **attractive** and acts along the line connecting the centers of two masses.
 
• It plays a critical role in the formation and structure of **galaxies, solar systems, and the universe itself**.
 
• Gravitational force also governs phenomena such as **tides**, which are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth's oceans.
 
• It is one of the weakest forces in nature but has an infinite range, making it significant on a **cosmic scale**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Spring Force**__

 __
 
• **Spring Force** is a contact force that occurs in objects like springs when they are stretched or compressed.
 
• The force exerted by a spring is governed by **Hooke's Law**, which states that the force is proportional to the displacement.
 
• This force is used in various applications, such as **shock absorbers**, mechanical clocks, and measuring devices like **spring balances**.
 
 
 
• **Friction**__
 __
 
• **Friction** is a contact force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact.
 
• It is critical in everyday activities like walking, driving, and holding objects.
 
• However, friction cannot act at a distance and is not responsible for celestial body motion.
 
 
 
• **Tension**__
 
 
• **Tension** is a force that arises in strings, ropes, or cables when they are pulled taut.
 
• This is a contact force and is commonly seen in structures like **bridges** or when lifting objects using ropes.
 
• It does not act at a distance and is not involved in the motion of celestial bodies.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disproportionation reaction?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cl2 + H2O → HCI + HOCI**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Disproportionation reactions involve the simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the same species within a chemical reaction.
 
• In the reaction **Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl**, chlorine (Cl₂) undergoes disproportionation as it is both oxidized to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and reduced to form hydrochloric acid (HCl).
 
• The oxidation state of chlorine in Cl₂ is 0. In HCl, it is reduced to -1, and in HOCl, it is oxidized to +1.
 
• This reaction occurs naturally in water when chlorine is dissolved, and is often used in water purification and disinfection processes.
 
• Disproportionation reactions are a subset of redox reactions and are characterized by the same element undergoing both gain and loss of electrons.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Oxidation:** It refers to the loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation state during a chemical reaction.
 
• **Reduction:** Reduction is the gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation state during a chemical reaction.
 
• **Oxidation State:** It is a number assigned to an element in a compound or ion that represents the number of electrons lost (positive oxidation state) or gained (negative oxidation state).
 
• **Redox Reactions:** These are reactions in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously, involving the transfer of electrons between species.
 
• **Applications of Disproportionation Reactions:** Such reactions are widely used in industrial processes, water treatment, and chemical synthesis (e.g., the production of bleaching agents and disinfectants).

questions.question: Which of the following materials is most suitable for making filaments in electric bulbs?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tungsten**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tungsten** is the most suitable material for making electric bulb filaments due to its **high melting point** of approximately 3422°C, which allows it to operate at high temperatures without melting.
 
• It has a very low rate of evaporation at high temperatures, ensuring a longer lifespan of the filament.
 
• Tungsten has excellent tensile strength, which prevents it from breaking easily when subjected to thermal expansion and contraction.
 
• Its high resistivity enables it to convert electrical energy into heat efficiently, producing bright light.
 
• When used in an inert gas-filled bulb, tungsten's performance is further enhanced by reducing filament evaporation and improving efficiency.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Properties of Tungsten:**

 
 
• The high melting point of tungsten makes it suitable for applications requiring heat resistance.
 
• Its density is around 19.3 g/cm³, making it one of the heaviest metals.
 
• Tungsten's low vapor pressure at high temperatures ensures minimal material loss.
 
 
 
• **Why Other Materials Are Not Suitable:**
 
 
• **Copper:** Low melting point (~1085°C) makes it unsuitable for high-temperature applications like filaments.
 
• **Aluminium:** Melts at approximately 660°C and lacks the durability required for filaments.
 
• **Iron:** Melting point (~1538°C) is higher than copper or aluminium but still insufficient compared to tungsten.
 
 
 
• **Inert Gas in Bulbs:** Modern electric bulbs are filled with inert gases like argon or a mixture of argon and nitrogen to prevent the oxidation of the tungsten filament and reduce evaporation.
 
• **Historical Background:** The use of tungsten in filaments was pioneered in the early 20th century, replacing earlier materials like carbon due to its superior properties.
 
• **Applications Beyond Bulbs:** Tungsten is also used in x-ray tubes, welding electrodes, and aerospace due to its heat-resistant properties.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about DNA and RNA is true?

options.text: DNA is not present in viruses.
DNA acts only as a messenger molecule.
RNA has multiple roles including catalytic functions.
RNA acts solely as genetic material in all living organisms.

questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**RNA has multiple roles including catalytic functions**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **RNA** is a versatile molecule that performs various functions essential for life.
 
• In addition to being a genetic material in certain organisms (like viruses), RNA also plays a major role in protein synthesis as **messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).**
 
• Certain types of RNA, such as **ribozymes**, exhibit **catalytic functions**. Ribozymes catalyze biochemical reactions, such as cleaving RNA molecules or forming peptide bonds during protein synthesis.
 
• The discovery of catalytic RNA challenged the traditional belief that only **proteins** could act as enzymes.
 
• RNA is involved in processes such as **gene regulation, splicing, and editing**, highlighting its multifunctional nature.
 
• The ability of RNA to fold into complex three-dimensional structures is crucial for its catalytic and regulatory roles.
 
• Examples of RNA molecules with catalytic functions include **self-splicing introns** and the **ribosome**, where rRNA catalyzes peptide bond formation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **DNA is not present in viruses**__

 __
 
• Some viruses, such as **retroviruses** (e.g., HIV), use RNA as their genetic material instead of DNA.
 
• However, many viruses, including **adenoviruses and herpesviruses**, contain DNA as their genetic material. Hence, the statement is incorrect.
 
 
 
• **DNA acts only as a messenger molecule**__
 __
 
• DNA is primarily the **repository of genetic information** in most organisms. It does not function as a messenger molecule; this role is performed by **RNA (mRNA).**
 
 
 
• **RNA acts solely as genetic material in all living organisms**__
 
 
• In most living organisms, **DNA** serves as the primary genetic material, while RNA plays supporting roles. Only certain viruses use RNA as their genetic material.

questions.question: What is the nature of wavefront from a point source in an isotropic medium?
questions.solution:
The Correct answer is __**Spherical**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **point source** emits light uniformly in all directions in an **isotropic medium**, where the medium has identical properties in every direction.
 
• The emitted light creates a wavefront that is equidistant from the point source at any given instant.
 
• The geometry of this wavefront is **spherical**, as it forms concentric spheres centered around the point source.
 
• Wavefronts are defined as surfaces of constant phase, and in the case of a point source, these surfaces expand radially outward, maintaining a spherical shape.
 
• The spherical wavefront is a fundamental concept in **optics** and is used to describe wave propagation in various applications.
 
• This behavior is explained by the **Huygens' Principle**, which states that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets, propagating outward.
 
• The spherical nature of the wavefront is important in many fields, including **physics**, **acoustics**, and **engineering**, as it helps in understanding wave behavior in isotropic media.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Elliptical**__

 __
 
• An **elliptical wavefront** is associated with sources that emit waves in an anisotropic medium or when the propagation is affected by external factors such as direction-dependent properties of the medium.
 
• Elliptical wavefronts are less common in nature compared to spherical wavefronts.
 
 
 
• **Cylindrical**__
 __
 
• **Cylindrical wavefronts** are generated by linear sources, such as a vibrating string or a slit in optics experiments.
 
• The wavefronts expand as concentric cylinders rather than spheres.
 
 
 
• **Plane**__
 
 
• **Plane wavefronts** occur when the source is very far away or when waves propagate in a single direction without divergence, such as lasers.
 
• In this case, the wavefronts appear as flat surfaces rather than curved ones.
